ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Twenty-four antipsychotic-naïve individuals at CHR-P aged 18-40 years were recruited from OASIS (Outreach and Support in South London), an early-intervention service within the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust, UK [43].

> CHR-P status was confirmed using the Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States (CAARMS) [44] and participants were required to be currently experiencing attenuated psychosis symptoms, defined as scoring 3 on the severity and frequency scoring system on P1-P4 of the CAARMS.

> Twenty-four HCs aged 18-40 years were recruited through public advertisements within the same geographical region.

> All participants were required to have capacity to consent, IQ>70 (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale III, shortened version [45]), no history of neurological disorders, and no current or past exposure to antipsychotic medication.

> Thirteen participants took part in both Study 1 and Study 2; nine of these participants took part in Study 1 first.

> Twenty-four antipsychotic-naïve individuals at CHR-P aged 18-40 years were recruited from the OASIS to participate in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design study.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

CHR-P status was confirmed using the Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States (CAARMS) [44] and participants were required to be currently experiencing attenuated psychosis symptoms, defined as scoring 3 on the severity and frequency scoring system on P1-P4 of the CAARMS.
Twenty-four HCs aged 18-40 years were recruited through public advertisements within the same geographical region.

All participants were required to have capacity to consent, IQ>70 (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale III, shortened version [45]), no history of neurological disorders, and no current or past exposure to antipsychotic medication.
Thirteen participants took part in both Study 1 and Study 2; nine of these participants took part in Study 1 first.
Twenty-four antipsychotic-naïve individuals at CHR-P aged 18-40 years were recruited from the OASIS to participate in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design study.
Thirteen participants took part in both Study 1 and Study 2; four of these participants took part in Study 2 first.
Diazepam or placebo was administered 60 minutes before scanning, and participants completed the ER40 during blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) fMRI.

Quantitative CBF maps for each participant were co-registered, segmented, and normalised to the MNI template and spatially smoothed (6mm FWHM) using the Automated Software for ASL Processing toolbox [57].
All participants provided written informed consent.

text.text: Deficits in social cognition, including facial emotion recognition (FER), are present in individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P).
Altered GABAergic and glutamatergic signalling within corticolimbic circuitry has been proposed to underlie FER deficits in psychosis.
We investigated FER performance and brain activation in CHR-P individuals, and whether pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic signalling with diazepam modulates these processes.
In Study 1, 24 antipsychotic-naïve CHR-P individuals and 24 healthy controls underwent fMRI while performing the Penn Emotion Recognition Task.
In Study 2, 24 antipsychotic-naïve CHR-P individuals participated in a randomised, double-blind, placebocontrolled, crossover study of 5mg diazepam versus placebo.
Threat-related FER performance and neural activation were compared between groups and drug conditions.
In Study 1, CHR-P individuals showed longer reaction times across emotions (n=22 vs n=23, p=0.01) and greater amygdala (pFWE=0.01) and hippocampal (pFWE=0.04) activation for neutral>fixation.
text.formatted: In Study 1, CHR-P individuals showed longer reaction times across emotions (n=22 vs n=23, p=0.01) and greater amygdala (pFWE=0.01) and hippocampal (pFWE=0.04) activation for neutral>fixation.

text.text: Lower amygdala activation for threat>neutral (pFWE=0.03) and non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.01), and lower hippocampal activation for non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.04) may reflect this elevated response to neutral faces.
text.formatted: Lower amygdala activation for threat>neutral (pFWE=0.03) and non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.01), and lower hippocampal activation for non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.04) may reflect this elevated response to neutral faces.

text.text: Follow-up analyses showed lower insula (pFWE=0.01) and medial prefrontal cortex activation (pFWE=0.02) for threat>fixation.
text.formatted: Follow-up analyses showed lower insula (pFWE=0.01) and medial prefrontal cortex activation (pFWE=0.02) for threat>fixation.

text.text: In Study 2, no significant drug effect on sensitivity was observed in the full sample (n=23), although secondary reduced-sample analyses, excluding one participant identified as influential, suggested improved overall sensitivity under diazepam (n=22; p=0.0499).
After adjusting for global cerebral blood flow, diazepam reduced midcingulate cortex activation during neutral>fixation (pFWE=0.04).
text.formatted: After adjusting for global cerebral blood flow, diazepam reduced midcingulate cortex activation during neutral>fixation (pFWE=0.04).

text.text: These findings highlight altered neural processing of neutral expressions in individuals at CHR-P, and suggest that aspects of emotion processing may be sensitive to GABAergic modulation.
Deficits in social cognition, particularly in interpreting socio-emotional cues, are a wellestablished feature of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SSDs) [1] [2] [3] [4].
text.formatted: Deficits in social cognition, particularly in interpreting socio-emotional cues, are a wellestablished feature of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SSDs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Difficulties with facial emotion recognition (FER) are associated with poor social and functional outcomes [5, 6], and may also contribute to the pathophysiology of psychosis.
text.formatted: Difficulties with facial emotion recognition (FER) are associated with poor social and functional outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>, and may also contribute to the pathophysiology of psychosis.

text.text: Aberrant processing of emotionally salient social cues, particularly threat-related, has been implicated in psychotic symptoms such as persecutory delusions [7], which are reported in about 55-77% of children and adolescents at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P) presenting to mental health services [8, 9].
text.formatted: Aberrant processing of emotionally salient social cues, particularly threat-related, has been implicated in psychotic symptoms such as persecutory delusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, which are reported in about 55-77% of children and adolescents at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P) presenting to mental health services <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, emotion processing may be an important domain for understanding both the clinical and functional manifestations of psychosis.
The CHR-P state describes individuals at elevated risk of developing psychosis, approximately 25% of whom transition to psychosis within 3 years of clinical presentation [10].
text.formatted: The CHR-P state describes individuals at elevated risk of developing psychosis, approximately 25% of whom transition to psychosis within 3 years of clinical presentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Individuals at CHR-P show moderate social-cognitive deficits relative to healthy individuals [4], including difficulties in recognising neutral and threat-related facial expressions such as anger, disgust, and fear [4, 11, 12].
text.formatted: Individuals at CHR-P show moderate social-cognitive deficits relative to healthy individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, including difficulties in recognising neutral and threat-related facial expressions such as anger, disgust, and fear <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: A recent meta-analysis further found more pronounced baseline emotion processing deficits in CHR-P individuals who subsequently transitioned to psychosis than those who did not [11], suggesting that characterising FER deficits and their neural correlates may provide insights into mechanisms associated with psychosis risk (14) (15) (16) (17) (18).
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis further found more pronounced baseline emotion processing deficits in CHR-P individuals who subsequently transitioned to psychosis than those who did not <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, suggesting that characterising FER deficits and their neural correlates may provide insights into mechanisms associated with psychosis risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: Functional neuroimaging studies in SSDs have implicated altered recruitment of corticolimbic regions during FER, including the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), fusiform gyrus, hippocampus, insula, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) [13] [14] [15] [16].
text.formatted: Functional neuroimaging studies in SSDs have implicated altered recruitment of corticolimbic regions during FER, including the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), fusiform gyrus, hippocampus, insula, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Findings in CHR-P have been less consistent.

A recent meta-analysis identified convergent alterations only in the posterior cingulate cortex at a lenient threshold [17], while individual studies have reported alterations in prefrontal, insular, thalamic, and inferior frontal regions [18] [19] [20] [21].
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis identified convergent alterations only in the posterior cingulate cortex at a lenient threshold <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, while individual studies have reported alterations in prefrontal, insular, thalamic, and inferior frontal regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: These findings raise the possibility of altered corticolimbic recruitment during FER in CHR-P, although the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear.
One proposed mechanism is disrupted balance between excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic neurotransmission [22].
text.formatted: One proposed mechanism is disrupted balance between excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic neurotransmission <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: In the hippocampus, reduced GABAergic interneuron function has been proposed to contribute to excitatory/inhibitory imbalance in SSDs [23] [24] [25] [26] [27].
text.formatted: In the hippocampus, reduced GABAergic interneuron function has been proposed to contribute to excitatory/inhibitory imbalance in SSDs <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Given its reciprocal connectivity with other corticolimbic regions involved in emotion processing, including the amygdala [28] [29] [30] [31], altered hippocampal GABAergic function may affect broader network function [13, 17, 32].
text.formatted: Given its reciprocal connectivity with other corticolimbic regions involved in emotion processing, including the amygdala <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>, altered hippocampal GABAergic function may affect broader network function <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>.

text.text: GABAergic signalling can be pharmacologically modulated with benzodiazepines such as diazepam, a positive allosteric modulator at the GABAA receptor that potentiates the effects of endogenous GABA [33].
text.formatted: GABAergic signalling can be pharmacologically modulated with benzodiazepines such as diazepam, a positive allosteric modulator at the GABAA receptor that potentiates the effects of endogenous GABA <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Benzodiazepines have been shown to modulate FER in healthy individuals [34] [35] [36], supporting a role for GABAergic inhibition in the neural mechanisms underlying emotion processing.
text.formatted: Benzodiazepines have been shown to modulate FER in healthy individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>, supporting a role for GABAergic inhibition in the neural mechanisms underlying emotion processing.

text.text: Enhancing GABAergic signalling may modulate FER performance and its neural circuitry, providing a pharmacological probe of GABAergic contributions to emotion-processing abnormalities in CHR-P.
Accordingly, we sought to determine whether threat-related FER is altered in individuals at CHR-P and whether it is modifiable through acute GABAergic modulation.
Signal Detection Theory (SDT) analyses were used to distinguish sensitivity from response bias [37, 38].
text.formatted: Signal Detection Theory (SDT) analyses were used to distinguish sensitivity from response bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38]</ref>.

text.text: In Study 1, we examined behavioural performance and corticolimbic activation during threatrelated FER in antipsychotic-naïve individuals at CHR-P and healthy controls (HCs).
We hypothesised that CHR-P individuals would show heightened threat processing and aberrant corticolimbic activation [7, 11, [39] [40] [41] [42].
text.formatted: We hypothesised that CHR-P individuals would show heightened threat processing and aberrant corticolimbic activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: In Study 2, we investigated whether 5 mg diazepam modulated threat-related FER in CHR-P. We hypothesised that diazepam would attenuate threat-related processing at behavioural and neural levels.

text.text: Participants viewed 60 faces expressing anger, fear, happiness, sadness or neutral expressions for 4000 ms and identified the displayed emotion by button-press on a joystick.
Variable intervals ranging from 2000-12000ms, weighted towards shorter intervals, displaying a complex fixation cross matched on facial perceptual qualities were interspersed throughout the trials.
For analysis, anger + fear were combined as threat, happy + sad were combined as non-threat, and neutral expressions were modelled separately [48].
text.formatted: For analysis, anger + fear were combined as threat, happy + sad were combined as non-threat, and neutral expressions were modelled separately <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref>.

text.text: Full task details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

T1-weighted structural and BOLD fMRI data were acquired in both studies.
Full acquisition parameters for each study are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Full ASL preprocessing details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
Behavioural outcomes included accuracy, false alarm rate (FAR), sensitivity (d'), criterion bias, and latency/reaction time.

Signal Detection Theory was used to distinguish sensitivity from response bias: d' reflects the ability to discriminate target from non-target stimuli, whereas criterion bias reflects the tendency to respond that a target is present [37].
text.formatted: Signal Detection Theory was used to distinguish sensitivity from response bias: d' reflects the ability to discriminate target from non-target stimuli, whereas criterion bias reflects the tendency to respond that a target is present <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: Detailed calculations for each parameter are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
Behavioural analyses were conducted using R Studio Version 2025.05.0+496.

Generalised linear mixed-effects models with a binomial distribution and logit link were used for accuracy and FAR, and linear mixed effects models were used for d', criterion bias, and reaction times.
Models included group (Study 1) or drug condition (Study 2), emotion, and their interaction, with participant ID included as a random effect.
Statistical significance was set at p<0.05, with Bonferroni correction for emotion-specific effects.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was set at p<0.05, with Bonferroni correction for emotion-specific effects.

text.text: Sensitivity analyses additionally examined the effects of age, sex, IQ, and anxiety in Study 1, and anxiety, fatigue and drug order in Study 2.
Further model specifications are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Directional emotion misattribution errors were compared between CHR-P individuals and HCs in Study 1, and between diazepam and placebo in Study 2 using generalised linear mixed effects models with a binomial distribution and logit link function.
Full model specifications are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
First-level analyses were conducted in SPM12 [56].

text.text: No significant drug effects were observed for other contrasts.
Our main findings were that individuals at CHR-P showed slower responses during facial emotion recognition and altered neural responses to emotional and neutral facial expressions.
Specifically, CHR-P individuals showed longer reaction times during FER compared to HC, but no significant differences in accuracy, FAR, sensitivity, or criterion bias.
At the neural level, CHR-P individuals showed greater activation near the amygdala-hippocampal border to neutral expressions and lower insula and mPFC activation for threat relative to fixation.
In Study 2, diazepam produced no significant behavioural effect in the primary analysis and no significant effects within the pre-specified ROIs.

Secondary analyses suggested greater overall sensitivity (d') following diazepam in a reduced sample and attenuated midcingulate cortex (MCC) responses to neutral expressions after adjustment for global CBF.
Overall, while diazepam did not normalise the alterations observed in CHR-P, the findings suggest that aspects of emotion processing may be sensitive to GABAergic modulation.

Individuals at CHR-P showed slower reaction times across emotions but no significant differences in accuracy, FAR, sensitivity, criterion bias, or directional misclassifications, contrary to our hypothesis of heightened behavioural threat processing.
Similar slower reaction times have been reported in SSDs [42, 60, 61] and may reflect greater processing demands despite otherwise comparable FER performance.

text.text: Contrary to our hypotheses, diazepam had no significant effects on emotion processing accuracy, FAR, sensitivity, criterion bias, or latency in the primary analysis.
In a secondary analysis adjusting for baseline anxiety, sensitivity was higher under diazepam, but this analysis excluded two participants with missing HAM-A data.
Repeating the unadjusted analysis in this reduced sample yielded a similar effect, suggesting that finding was attributable to participant exclusion rather than anxiety adjustment.
Post-hoc influence analyses identified one of these participants as potentially influential, and exclusion of this participant alone also resulted in a nominally significant effect.

Thus, these findings suggest a potential increase in overall emotion processing sensitivity under diazepam, although this effect was sensitive to participant inclusion and should be interpreted with caution.
No diazepam effects were observed for criterion bias, directional misattribution, or emotionspecific outcomes.

If replicated, the selective effect on sensitivity could suggest improved discrimination rather than altered response tendencies, although the processes underlying this behavioural finding remain inconclusive.

Previous work in healthy individuals similarly reported that 5 mg diazepam did not affect emotion processing accuracy or latency [75], whereas higher doses of diazepam have altered recognition of threatening emotions but also produced sedation [35, 36].

At the neural level, diazepam did not significantly affect threat processing within the prespecified ROIs.
However, in a secondary whole-brain analysis adjusting for global CBF, diazepam reduced MCC activation to neutral expressions.
The MCC has been implicated in salience processing [76], and aberrant salience attribution to irrelevant or ambiguous stimuli is proposed to play an important role in psychosis risk [77] [78] [79].

The absence of ROI effects differs from previous pharmacological imaging studies in healthy individuals using 10 mg diazepam [34] and first-degree relatives of individuals with schizophrenia using 1mg alprazolam [49], which reported benzodiazepine-related modulation of amygdala, hippocampus, ACC and insula responses.

text.text: Higher benzodiazepine doses may also produce greater neural effects but increase sedation-related confounding.
Overall, the absence of effects within the pre-specified corticolimbic ROIs provides little evidence that 5 mg diazepam robustly modulated the hypothesised circuitry.
The whole-brain MCC finding nevertheless suggests that neural responses to neutral expressions may be sensitive to acute GABAergic modulation.
Across both studies, neutral facial expressions emerged as a potentially informative condition for understanding altered social-emotional processing in CHR-P.

To our knowledge, this was the first study to apply Signal Detection Theory to characterise FER in individuals at CHR-P and the first to investigate the acute effects of diazepam on FER and its neural correlates in this population.
The use of SDT across both studies enabled emotion processing performance to be characterised beyond conventional accuracy metrics, by distinguishing sensitivity from criterion bias.
Nevertheless, several limitations should also be considered.
Some significant findings arose from post-hoc, sensitivity, or supplementary analyses.

In Study 1, threat>fixation and non-threat>fixation analyses were conducted posthoc; in Study 2, the behavioural effect emerged only in reduced-sample analyses, and the MCC effect only after adjustment for global CBF in a secondary analysis.

text.text: These findings should therefore be interpreted with caution and require replication.

The ER40 also showed ceiling or floor effects for some accuracy and FAR metrics, which may have limited sensitivity to subtle behavioural differences and constrained derived d' and criterion bias estimates.
Combining anger and fear into a threat category, and sadness and happiness into a non-threat category, increased trial numbers but may have obscured emotion-specific effects.

Both studies included relatively small sample sizes, 13 CHR-P participants contributed to both studies, there were significant differences in ethnicities between CHR-P and HCs in Study 1, and Study 2 lacked a HC group, preventing assessment of whether diazepam shifted responses towards a normative pattern.

Finally, the 5 mg diazepam dose was selected to minimise sedation; future pharmaco-fMRI studies could use dose-response designs and more selective GABAA receptor compounds to better delineate GABAergic effects on emotion processing in CHR-P.

Emotion processing in individuals at CHR-P is associated with altered corticolimbic activation, particularly elevated amygdala-hippocampal responses to neutral facial expressions, despite largely comparable behavioural performance to healthy controls.

Diazepam did not significantly affect behavioural performance in the primary analysis or activation within the prespecified corticolimbic ROIs, although secondary analyses suggested increased overall emotion sensitivity and reduced MCC responses to neutral expressions.
These findings highlight the potential relevance of neutral, socially ambiguous facial expressions in CHR-P and suggest that aspects of emotion processing may be sensitive to GABAergic modulation.
